title: DPDP Act 2023 & Rules 2025
subtitle: 30 exam-oriented questions across three sets, with explanations and exam traps.
description: Practice the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and DPDP Rules, 2025 for Bank SO IT examinations.
source: Reconstructed question bank supplied by the user. Legal claims, commencement timelines and the flagged items require final review against official government documents before public release.
instructions: 30 questions · 1 mark each · no negative marking.
Questions 1–10, 11–20 and 21–30 form three separate sets.
Question 10 is multi-select; all correct options and no incorrect options are required for the mark.
Explanations and exam traps appear only after submission.
This educational practice quiz is not legal advice.

questions.question: A bank determines why customers’ personal data is collected and how it will be processed. Under the DPDP Act, what is the bank in this situation?

options.text: Data Principal
Data Fiduciary
Data Processor
Consent Manager

questions.explanation: A Data Fiduciary determines the purpose and means of processing personal data. A bank making these decisions is acting as a Data Fiduciary.
questions.importantPoint: A Data Fiduciary determines the purpose and means of processing personal data.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse a Data Fiduciary with a Data Processor. A processor processes personal data on behalf of a fiduciary.
questions.hint: Identify the exact statutory definition, duty, section or commencement group being tested. Eliminate options that overstate the rule or confuse it with a different provision.

questions.question: The DPDP Act may apply to processing of digital personal data outside India when which condition is satisfied?

options.text: The processing is connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals within India.
The company has any employee who is an Indian citizen.
The company uses software developed in India.
The company maintains a bank account in India.

questions.explanation: The Act has an extraterritorial application provision for processing outside India when connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals within the territory of India.
questions.importantPoint: The Act has an extraterritorial application provision for processing outside India when connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals within the territory of India.
questions.examTrap: Do not assume that every foreign company is automatically covered. Check the statutory territorial-scope conditions.

questions.question: Which combination best describes valid consent under the DPDP Act?

options.text: Implied consent in every situation
Free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous consent indicated by clear affirmative action
Consent obtained only through a signed paper document
Consent obtained through a preselected checkbox in every case

questions.explanation: The Act establishes requirements for valid consent. It must be a clear affirmative action and meet the prescribed statutory characteristics.
questions.importantPoint: The Act establishes requirements for valid consent.
questions.examTrap: A preselected checkbox or silence should not automatically be treated as valid consent.

questions.question: Under the DPDP Act, an individual to whom personal data relates is known as:

questions.importantPoint: A Data Principal is the individual to whom the personal data relates.

questions.question: A customer requests erasure of personal data held by a bank. What should the bank consider before deleting the data?

options.text: The bank must always delete all data immediately.
The bank can never delete financial records.
Applicable legal retention requirements and the relevant provisions of the DPDP Act.
The customer’s request can always be ignored.

questions.explanation: The right to erasure must be read alongside applicable legal requirements. A bank may have separate statutory or regulatory obligations to retain particular records.
questions.importantPoint: The right to erasure must be read alongside applicable legal requirements.
questions.examTrap: Erasure is not an unconditional requirement to destroy records that must lawfully be retained.

questions.question: Can a Data Principal withdraw consent under the DPDP Act?

options.text: No, consent is permanent once granted.
Only the Data Fiduciary can withdraw consent.
Yes, consent can be withdrawn, and withdrawal should be as easy as giving consent.
Only the Data Protection Board can withdraw consent.

questions.explanation: The Act recognises the right to withdraw consent. The process for withdrawal should be comparable in ease to the process for giving consent.
questions.importantPoint: The Act recognises the right to withdraw consent.
questions.examTrap: Withdrawal does not automatically make previous lawful processing unlawful. Also consider applicable legal obligations and the consequences specified in the Act.

questions.question:
Which of the following are recognised rights of a Data Principal under the DPDP Act?

Select all correct options.

options.text: Right to correction and completion of personal data, subject to applicable provisions
Right to grievance redressal
Unrestricted access to every internal document of a Data Fiduciary
Right to nominate another individual, subject to applicable provisions

questions.explanation: The Act recognises rights including correction and completion, grievance redressal, and nomination, subject to applicable provisions. It does not create a general right to inspect every internal document of an organisation.
questions.importantPoint: The Act recognises rights including correction and completion, grievance redressal, and nomination, subject to applicable provisions.
questions.examTrap: This is a multi-select question. Do not select an option simply because it sounds like a privacy right. Read the exact statutory right.  ---  # SET 2: PENALTIES, BOARD, EXEMPTIONS AND BANKING/IT SCENARIOS

questions.question: Before imposing a penalty under the DPDP Act, which procedural safeguard is relevant to the Data Protection Board's inquiry and penalty process?

options.text: The Board must obtain approval from every affected Data Principal.
The concerned person must be given an opportunity of being heard in accordance with the applicable statutory procedure.
The Board must conduct a criminal trial in every case.

questions.explanation: The Act establishes an inquiry process and requires the relevant procedural safeguards to be followed before the Board reaches its decision.
questions.importantPoint: The Act establishes an inquiry process and requires the relevant procedural safeguards to be followed before the Board reaches its decision.
questions.examTrap: A complaint or alleged contravention does not mean that the maximum penalty is imposed automatically.

questions.question: A bank experiences a personal data breach and is accused both of failing to implement reasonable security safeguards and of failing to notify the required parties. How should the potential contraventions be analysed?

options.text: Treat both failures as one identical contravention with one automatically fixed penalty.
Analyse the distinct statutory obligations and applicable Schedule entries separately; the maximum amounts are not automatically imposed or summed.
Apply only the smaller maximum penalty in every case.
Assume that no penalty can apply if the breach was accidental.

questions.explanation: Security safeguards and breach notification are separate obligations. Any penalty determination must follow the applicable statutory process and consider the circumstances of the contraventions.
questions.importantPoint: Security safeguards and breach notification are separate obligations.
questions.examTrap: Two possible contraventions do not mean that both maximum penalties are automatically imposed.

questions.question: A Data Fiduciary gives a voluntary undertaking to the Data Protection Board under Section 32, and the undertaking is accepted. What is the significance if the undertaking is subsequently breached?

options.text: The undertaking automatically cancels all liability under the Act.
Breach of the accepted undertaking can attract consequences under Section 32, subject to the statutory conditions.
The undertaking has no legal significance.
The Data Principal must personally impose the penalty.

questions.explanation: The Act provides for voluntary undertakings and consequences for breaching an accepted undertaking. The applicable statutory conditions and penalty provisions must be considered.
questions.importantPoint: The Act provides for voluntary undertakings and consequences for breaching an accepted undertaking.

questions.question: A bank claims that a particular processing activity is exempt from certain DPDP Act obligations. What is the correct approach?

Examine the relevant exemption provision, its conditions, and the facts of the processing activity.

questions.question: A Data Fiduciary is found to have contravened a provision of the DPDP Act. Does the maximum penalty listed in the Schedule automatically become the final penalty?

options.text: Yes, the maximum is mandatory in every case.
Yes, if the organisation is a bank.
No, the applicable statutory process and relevant factors must be considered.
No penalty can ever be imposed on an organisation.

questions.explanation: The Schedule specifies maximum penalties for listed contraventions. It does not mean that the maximum amount is automatically imposed in every case.
